core: The two defining properties of a public good: non-rival (one person's use does not reduce what is available to others) and non-excludable (it is costly or impossible to prevent non-payers from using it)
The free-rider problem: when a good is non-excludable, individuals have an incentive to let others pay and consume it anyway, so voluntary contributions fall short
Why private markets under-provide public goods (a market failure) and why this motivates government provision funded by taxes
Classic examples of public goods: national defense, a lighthouse, public fireworks, and basic research

The 2x2 classification of goods by rivalry x excludability: private goods (rival, excludable), public goods (non-rival, non-excludable), common resources (rival, non-excludable), and club goods / artificially scarce goods (non-rival, excludable)
The tragedy of the commons attributed to Garrett Hardin (1968), and Elinor Ostrom's finding that communities can self-govern common-pool resources
supporting: The distinction between a pure public good and goods that are only partially non-rival or non-excludable
That non-excludability, not non-rivalry alone, is what prevents a private firm from charging and thus drives the market failure
outOfScope: Externalities as a distinct market failure (its own topic): contrasted briefly but not owned here
Fiscal policy and how governments raise and spend tax revenue (named, handed off)
Incentives as a standalone foundational concept (named, handed off)
Detailed welfare/efficiency analysis and the formal Samuelson condition for optimal public-good provision

claims.claim: A public good has two defining characteristics: it is non-rival (when one person uses it, others can still use it) and non-excludable (it is costly or impossible to exclude someone from using it, and thus hard to charge for).
The free-rider problem is the situation in which people have an incentive to let others pay for a public good and then use it themselves; if enough people free-ride, the good may never be provided.

Because a public good is non-excludable, private firms cannot reliably charge users and therefore cannot profitably supply it, so competitive markets tend to under-provide public goods; this market failure is a standard economic rationale for government provision financed by taxes.

National defense is a textbook example of a public good: it is non-excludable (it protects even those who disagree with defense policy or pay no tax) and non-rival (one resident's protection does not reduce another's); fire and police services and basic research are treated similarly.

Goods can be classified on two axes, excludability and rivalry, giving four types: private goods (rival and excludable, e.g. food, clothing), public goods (non-rival and non-excludable, e.g. national defense), common resources / common goods (rival but non-excludable, e.g. ocean fish stocks), and club goods (non-rival but excludable, e.g. cable television).

Common resources are rival but non-excludable, which can lead to the 'tragedy of the commons' — a phrase Garrett Hardin used in a 1968 article in Science to describe how self-interested users overexploit a shared resource beyond its carrying capacity.

Elinor Ostrom was awarded the 2009 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons; her research documented that communities can and do successfully self-govern common-pool resources without top-down control or privatization.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'pure' public goods are common in reality
positions: Standard textbook treatment lists national defense, lighthouses, and public fireworks as pure public goods
Some economists (e.g. Coase on the lighthouse) argue several textbook examples have historically been provided privately, so pure non-excludability is rarer than claimed
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents national defense as the cleanest pure case and frames lighthouses/fireworks as classic illustrations, noting that excludability is a matter of degree rather than a strict binary.
